document.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

4C58E1B0DFE701317BB168A86D17958E.description: Relating the choice of measures of center and variability to the shape of the data distribution and the context in which the data were gathered.

4C58A010DFE701317BB068A86D17958E.description: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.

4C585D10DFE701317BAF68A86D17958E.description: Describing the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement.

4C57C6B0DFE701317BAD68A86D17958E.description: Summarize numerical data sets in relation to their context, such as by:

4C578450DFE701317BAC68A86D17958E.description: Display numerical data in plots on a number line, including dot plots, histograms, and box plots.

4C56EB60DFE701317BAA68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that a measure of center for a numerical data set summarizes all of its values with a single number, while a measure of variation describes how its values vary with a single number.

4C569D40DFE701317BA968A86D17958E.description: Understand that a set of data collected to answer a statistical question has a distribution which can be described by its center, spread, and overall shape.

comments: For example, "How old am I?" is not a statistical question, but "How old are the students in my school?" is a statistical question because one anticipates variability in students' ages.
4C564B40DFE701317BA868A86D17958E.description: Recognize a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the data related to the question and accounts for it in the answers.

4C5562B0DFE701317BA568A86D17958E.description: Use variables to represent two quantities in a real-world problem that change in relationship to one another; write an equation to express one quantity, thought of as the dependent variable, in terms of the other quantity, thought of as the independent variable. Analyze the relationship between the dependent and independent variables using graphs and tables, and relate these to the equation.
comments: For example, in a problem involving motion at constant speed, list and graph ordered pairs of distances and times, and write the equation d = 65t to represent the relationship between distance and time.

4C551740DFE701317BA468A86D17958E.description: Represent and analyze quantitative relationships between dependent and independent variables.

4C54B2B0DFE701317BA368A86D17958E.description: Write an inequality of the form x > c or x < c to represent a constraint or condition in a real-world or mathematical problem. Recognize that inequalities of the form x > c or x < c have infinitely many solutions; represent solutions of such inequalities on number line diagrams.

4C545FC0DFE701317BA268A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by writing and solving equations of the form x + p = q and px = q for cases in which p, q and x are all nonnegative rational numbers.

4C540C50DFE701317BA168A86D17958E.description: Use variables to represent numbers and write expressions when solving a real-world or mathematical problem; understand that a variable can represent an unknown number, or, depending on the purpose at hand, any number in a specified set.

4C53AE10DFE701317BA068A86D17958E.description: Understand solving an equation or inequality as a process of answering a question: which values from a specified set, if any, make the equation or inequality true? Use substitution to determine whether a given number in a specified set makes an equation or inequality true.

4C536AE0DFE701317B9F68A86D17958E.description: Reason about and solve one-variable equations and inequalities.

comments: For example, the expressions y + y + y and 3y are equivalent because they name the same number regardless of which number y stands for.
4C5325D0DFE701317B9E68A86D17958E.description: Identify when two expressions are equivalent (i.e., when the two expressions name the same number regardless of which value is substituted into them).

comments: For example, apply the distributive property to the expression 3 (2 + x) to produce the equivalent expression 6 + 3x; apply the distributive property to the expression 24x + 18y to produce the equivalent expression 6 (4x + 3y); apply properties of operations to y + y + y to produce the equivalent expression 3y.
4C52DF00DFE701317B9D68A86D17958E.description: Apply the properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.

4C529330DFE701317B9C68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate expressions at specific values of their variables. Include expressions that arise from formulas used in real-world problems. Perform arithmetic operations, including those involving whole-number exponents, in the conventional order when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order (Order of Operations).
comments: For example, use the formulas V = s³ and A = 6 s² to find the volume and surface area of a cube with sides of length s = 1/2.

4C5233D0DFE701317B9B68A86D17958E.description: Identify parts of an expression using mathematical terms (sum, term, product, factor, quotient, coefficient); view one or more parts of an expression as a single entity.
comments: For example, describe the expression 2 (8 + 7) as a product of two factors; view (8 + 7) as both a single entity and a sum of two terms.
For example, express the calculation "Subtract y from 5" as 5 - y.
4C51E390DFE701317B9A68A86D17958E.description: Write expressions that record operations with numbers and with letters standing for numbers.

4C518800DFE701317B9968A86D17958E.description: Write, read, and evaluate expressions in which letters stand for numbers.

4C5140D0DFE701317B9868A86D17958E.description: Write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents.

4C50F780DFE701317B9768A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of arithmetic to algebraic expressions.

4C505B10DFE701317B9568A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane. Include use of coordinates and absolute value to find distances between points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate.

comments: For example, recognize that an account balance less than -30 dollars represents a debt greater than 30 dollars.
4C5016D0DFE701317B9468A86D17958E.description: Distinguish comparisons of absolute value from statements about order.

4C4FCEB0DFE701317B9368A86D17958E.description: Understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from 0 on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude for a positive or negative quantity in a real-world situation.
comments: For example, for an account balance of -30 dollars, write |-30| = 30 to describe the size of the debt in dollars.

4C4F8390DFE701317B9268A86D17958E.description: Write, interpret, and explain statements of order for rational numbers in real-world contexts.
comments: For example, write -3 °C > -7 °C to express the fact that -3 °C is warmer than -7 °C.

4C4F2DF0DFE701317B9168A86D17958E.description: Interpret statements of inequality as statements about the relative position of two numbers on a number line diagram.
comments: For example, interpret -3 > -7 as a statement that -3 is located to the right of -7 on a number line oriented from left to right.

4C4ED430DFE701317B9068A86D17958E.description: Understand ordering and absolute value of rational numbers.

4C4E83B0DFE701317B8F68A86D17958E.description: Find and position integers and other rational numbers on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram; find and position pairs of integers and other rational numbers on a coordinate plane.

4C4E3CA0DFE701317B8E68A86D17958E.description: Understand signs of numbers in ordered pairs as indicating locations in quadrants of the coordinate plane; recognize that when two ordered pairs differ only by signs, the locations of the points are related by reflections across one or both axes.

4C4DF9B0DFE701317B8D68A86D17958E.description: Recognize opposite signs of numbers as indicating locations on opposite sides of 0 on the number line; recognize that the opposite of the opposite of a number is the number itself, e.g., -(-3) = 3, and that 0 is its own opposite.

4C4DB580DFE701317B8C68A86D17958E.description: Understand a rational number as a point on the number line. Extend number line diagrams and coordinate axes familiar from previous grades to represent points on the line and in the plane with negative number coordinates.

4C4D6BE0DFE701317B8B68A86D17958E.description: Understand that positive and negative numbers are used together to describe quantities having opposite directions or values (e.g., temperature above/below zero, elevation above/below sea level, credits/debits, positive/negative electric charge); use positive and negative numbers to represent quantities in real-world contexts, explaining the meaning of 0 in each situation.

4C4D1BB0DFE701317B8A68A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of numbers to the system of rational numbers.

4C4CBF40DFE701317B8968A86D17958E.description: Find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers less than or equal to 100 and the least common multiple of two whole numbers less than or equal to 12. Use the distributive property to express a sum of two whole numbers 1—100 with a common factor as a multiple of a sum of two whole numbers with no common factor.
comments: For example, express 36 + 8 as 4 (9 + 2).

4C4C6360DFE701317B8868A86D17958E.description: Fluently add, subtract, multiply, and divide multi-digit decimals using the standard algorithm for each operation.

4C4C1610DFE701317B8768A86D17958E.description: Fluently divide multi-digit numbers using the standard algorithm.

4C4BD4E0DFE701317B8668A86D17958E.description: Compute fluently with multi-digit numbers and find common factors and multiples.

4C4B8DD0DFE701317B8568A86D17958E.description: Interpret and compute quotients of fractions, and solve word problems involving division of fractions by fractions, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.
comments: For example, create a story context for (2/3) ÷ (3/4) and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient; use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that (2/3) ÷ (3/4) = 8/9 because 3/4 of 8/9 is 2/3. (In general, (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = ad/bc.) How much chocolate will each person get if 3 people share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally? How many 3/4-cup servings are in 2/3 of a cup of yogurt? How wide is a rectangular strip of land with length 3/4 mi and area 1/2 square mi?

4C4B4000DFE701317B8468A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to divide fractions by fractions.

4C4ABA40DFE701317B8268A86D17958E.description: Use ratio reasoning to convert measurement units; manipulate and transform units appropriately when multiplying or dividing quantities.

4C4A75A0DFE701317B8168A86D17958E.description: Find a percent of a quantity as a rate per 100 (e.g., 30% of a quantity means 30/100 times the quantity); solve problems involving finding the whole, given a part and the percent.

comments: For example, if it took 7 hours to mow 4 lawns, then at that rate, how many lawns could be mowed in 35 hours? At what rate were lawns being mowed?
4C4A2F10DFE701317B8068A86D17958E.description: Solve unit rate problems including those involving unit pricing and constant speed.

4C49E580DFE701317B7F68A86D17958E.description: Make tables of equivalent ratios relating quantities with whole number measurements, find missing values in the tables, and plot the pairs of values on the coordinate plane. Use tables to compare ratios.

4C4991B0DFE701317B7E68A86D17958E.description: Use ratio and rate reasoning to solve real-world and mathematical problems, e.g., by reasoning about tables of equivalent ratios, tape diagrams, double number line diagrams, or equations.

4C492130DFE701317B7D68A86D17958E.description: Understand the concept of a unit rate a/b associated with a ratio a:b with b ≠ 0, and use rate language in the context of a ratio relationship.
comments: Expectations for unit rates in this grade are limited to non-complex fractions.
For example, "This recipe has a ratio of 3 cups of flour to 4 cups of sugar, so there is 3/4 cup of flour for each cup of sugar." "We paid $75 for 15 hamburgers, which is a rate of $5 per hamburger."

4C48DF50DFE701317B7C68A86D17958E.description: Understand the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities.
comments: For example, "The ratio of wings to beaks in the bird house at the zoo was 2:1, because for every 2 wings there was 1 beak." "For every vote candidate A received, candidate C received nearly three votes."

4C489E70DFE701317B7B68A86D17958E.description: Understand ratio concepts and use ratio reasoning to solve problems.

4C4819A0DFE701317B7968A86D17958E.description: Represent three-dimensional figures using nets made up of rectangles and triangles, and use the nets to find the surface area of these figures. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

4C47D0F0DFE701317B7868A86D17958E.description: Draw polygons in the coordinate plane given coordinates for the vertices; use coordinates to find the length of a side joining points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

4C478480DFE701317B7768A86D17958E.description: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with fractional edge lengths by packing it with unit cubes of the appropriate unit fraction edge lengths, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths of the prism. Apply the formulas V = l w h and V = b h to find volumes of right rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

4C4742C0DFE701317B7668A86D17958E.description: Find the area of right triangles, other triangles, special quadrilaterals, and polygons by composing into rectangles or decomposing into triangles and other shapes; apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

4C46FEF0DFE701317B7568A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area, surface area, and volume.

4C4664C0DFE701317B7368A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.
4C4615C0DFE701317B7268A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.

comments: Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
4C44C700DFE701317B6E68A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

4C4422C0DFE701317B6C68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Rhode Island K-12 Grade Span Expectations in Engineering and Technology

4E64C660DFE701317FC068A86D17958E.description: recognizing that there are specialized tools for different areas of engineering and technology.

4E648240DFE701317FBF68A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate an understanding of selecting appropriate tools by:

4E643C40DFE701317FBE68A86D17958E.description: Select and utilize appropriate tools to measure, design, and implement specific technologies.

4E63FB70DFE701317FBD68A86D17958E.description: making connections between the different areas of engineering and technology (e.g. recognize that transportation technologies are involved in construction).

4E63B170DFE701317FBC68A86D17958E.description: identifying community workers in the areas of engineering and technology. (e.g. bus driver in the area of transportation)

4E636280DFE701317FBB68A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate an understanding of the areas of engineering and technology by:

4E631FC0DFE701317FBA68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that there are various areas in engineering and technology.
comments: The Areas of Engineering and Technology as identified by the International Technology Engineering and Education Association are: Medical, Agricultural and Biotechnologies, Energy and Power, Information and Communication, Transportation, Manufacturing, and Construction.

4E62DC50DFE701317FB968A86D17958E.description: The designed world community selects and uses appropriate technologies.

4E6292B0DFE701317FB868A86D17958E.description: comparing and contrasting various design solutions (e.g. bus vs. race car).

4E6243A0DFE701317FB768A86D17958E.description: asking questions and making observations of design solutions (e.g. comparing toothbrush designs).

4E61F370DFE701317FB668A86D17958E.description: experimenting/exploring with various simple machines (e.g. wheels, axles, gears, pulleys) to demonstrate their uses and discuss their differences.

document.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

comments: For example, use random digits as a simulation tool to approximate the answer to the question: If 40% of donors have type A blood, what is the probability that it will take at least 4 donors to find one with type A blood?
4C81CA30DFE701317BF468A86D17958E.description: Design and use a simulation to generate frequencies for compound events.

4C8182C0DFE701317BF368A86D17958E.description: Represent sample spaces for compound events using methods such as organized lists, tables and tree diagrams. For an event described in everyday language (e.g., "rolling double sixes"), identify the outcomes in the sample space which compose the event.

4C813E40DFE701317BF268A86D17958E.description: Understand that, just as with simple events, the probability of a compound event is the fraction of outcomes in the sample space for which the compound event occurs.

4C80F1B0DFE701317BF168A86D17958E.description: Find probabilities of compound events using organized lists, tables, tree diagrams, and simulation.

4C809B80DFE701317BF068A86D17958E.description: Develop a probability model (which may not be uniform) by observing frequencies in data generated from a chance process.
comments: For example, find the approximate probability that a spinning penny will land heads up or that a tossed paper cup will land open-end down. Do the outcomes for the spinning penny appear to be equally likely based on the observed frequencies?
For example, if a student is selected at random from a class, find the probability that Jane will be selected and the probability that a girl will be selected.
4C805260DFE701317BEF68A86D17958E.description: Develop a uniform probability model by assigning equal probability to all outcomes, and use the model to determine probabilities of events.

4C8006F0DFE701317BEE68A86D17958E.description: Develop a probability model and use it to find probabilities of events. Compare probabilities from a model to observed frequencies; if the agreement is not good, explain possible sources of the discrepancy.

4C7FBCD0DFE701317BED68A86D17958E.description: Approximate the probability of a chance event by collecting data on the chance process that produces it and observing its long-run relative frequency, and predict the approximate relative frequency given the probability.
comments: For example, when rolling a number cube 600 times, predict that a 3 or 6 would be rolled roughly 200 times, but probably not exactly 200 times.

4C7F7640DFE701317BEC68A86D17958E.description: Understand that the probability of a chance event is a number between 0 and 1 that expresses the likelihood of the event occurring. Larger numbers indicate greater likelihood. A probability near 0 indicates an unlikely event, a probability around 1/2 indicates an event that is neither unlikely nor likely, and a probability near 1 indicates a likely event.

4C7F2D00DFE701317BEB68A86D17958E.description: Investigate chance processes and develop, use, and evaluate probability models.

4C7EDE40DFE701317BEA68A86D17958E.description: Use measures of center and measures of variability for numerical data from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.
comments: For example, decide whether the words in a chapter of a seventh-grade science book are generally longer than the words in a chapter of a fourth-grade science book.

4C7E9A40DFE701317BE968A86D17958E.description: Informally assess the degree of visual overlap of two numerical data distributions with similar variabilities, measuring the difference between the centers by expressing it as a multiple of a measure of variability.
comments: For example, the mean height of players on the basketball team is 10 cm greater than the mean height of players on the soccer team, about twice the variability (mean absolute deviation) on either team; on a dot plot, the separation between the two distributions of heights is noticeable.

4C7E5650DFE701317BE868A86D17958E.description: Draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.

4C7E1000DFE701317BE768A86D17958E.description: Use data from a random sample to draw inferences about a population with an unknown characteristic of interest. Generate multiple samples (or simulated samples) of the same size to gauge the variation in estimates or predictions.
comments: For example, estimate the mean word length in a book by randomly sampling words from the book; predict the winner of a school election based on randomly sampled survey data. Gauge how far off the estimate or prediction might be.

4C7DCA80DFE701317BE668A86D17958E.description: Understand that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a sample of the population; generalizations about a population from a sample are valid only if the sample is representative of that population. Understand that random sampling tends to produce representative samples and support valid inferences.

4C7D7810DFE701317BE568A86D17958E.description: Use random sampling to draw inferences about a population.

comments: For example: As a salesperson, you are paid $50 per week plus $3 per sale. This week you want your pay to be at least $100. Write an inequality for the number of sales you need to make, and describe the solutions.
4C7CD410DFE701317BE368A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form px + q > r or px + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem.

4C7C8650DFE701317BE268A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems leading to equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Solve equations of these forms fluently. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach.
comments: For example, the perimeter of a rectangle is 54 cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width?

4C7C3D10DFE701317BE168A86D17958E.description: Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities.

comments: For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50. If you want to place a towel bar 9 3/4 inches long in the center of a door that is 27 1/2 inches wide, you will need to place the bar about 9 inches from each edge; this estimate can be used as a check on the exact computation.
4C7BE5C0DFE701317BE068A86D17958E.description: Solve multi-step real-life and mathematical problems posed with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals), using tools strategically. Apply properties of operations to calculate with numbers in any form; convert between forms as appropriate; and assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies.

4C7B9920DFE701317BDF68A86D17958E.description: Solve real-life and mathematical problems using numerical and algebraic expressions and equations.

4C7B5310DFE701317BDE68A86D17958E.description: Understand that rewriting an expression in different forms in a problem context can shed light on the problem and how the quantities in it are related.
comments: For example, a + 0.05a = 1.05a means that "increase by 5%" is the same as "multiply by 1.05."

4C7B0DF0DFE701317BDD68A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add, subtract, factor, and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients.

4C7AC770DFE701317BDC68A86D17958E.description: Use properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.

comments: Computations with rational numbers extend the rules for manipulating fractions to complex fractions.
4C7A2910DFE701317BDA68A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the four operations with rational numbers.

4C79D8E0DFE701317BD968A86D17958E.description: Convert a rational number to a decimal using long division; know that the decimal form of a rational number terminates in 0s or eventually repeats.

4C7996F0DFE701317BD868A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide rational numbers.

4C7955F0DFE701317BD768A86D17958E.description: Understand that integers can be divided, provided that the divisor is not zero, and every quotient of integers (with non-zero divisor) is a rational number. If p and q are integers, then -(p/q) = (-p)/q = p/(-q). Interpret quotients of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

4C791360DFE701317BD668A86D17958E.description: Understand that multiplication is extended from fractions to rational numbers by requiring that operations continue to satisfy the properties of operations, particularly the distributive property, leading to products such as (-1)(-1) = 1 and the rules for multiplying signed numbers. Interpret products of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

4C78CD70DFE701317BD568A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division and of fractions to multiply and divide rational numbers.

4C788450DFE701317BD468A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract rational numbers.

4C783440DFE701317BD368A86D17958E.description: Understand subtraction of rational numbers as adding the additive inverse, p - q = p + (-q). Show that the distance between two rational numbers on the number line is the absolute value of their difference, and apply this principle in real-world contexts.

4C77EE80DFE701317BD268A86D17958E.description: Understand p + q as the number located a distance |q| from p, in the positive or negative direction depending on whether q is positive or negative. Show that a number and its opposite have a sum of 0 (are additive inverses). Interpret sums of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

4C77A850DFE701317BD168A86D17958E.description: Describe situations in which opposite quantities combine to make 0.
comments: For example, a hydrogen atom has 0 charge because its two constituents are oppositely charged.

4C7764E0DFE701317BD068A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of addition and subtraction to add and subtract rational numbers; represent addition and subtraction on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram.

4C772050DFE701317BCF68A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of operations with fractions to add, subtract, multiply, and divide rational numbers.

4C768210DFE701317BCD68A86D17958E.description: Use proportional relationships to solve multistep ratio and percent problems.
comments: Examples: simple interest, tax, markups and markdowns, gratuities and commissions, fees, percent increase and decrease, percent error.

4C763F90DFE701317BCC68A86D17958E.description: Explain what a point (x, y) on the graph of a proportional relationship means in terms of the situation, with special attention to the points (0, 0) and (1, r) where r is the unit rate.

comments: For example, if total cost t is proportional to the number n of items purchased at a constant price p, the relationship between the total cost and the number of items can be expressed as t = pn.

4C75A370DFE701317BCA68A86D17958E.description: Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships.

4C754B50DFE701317BC968A86D17958E.description: Decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship, e.g., by testing for equivalent ratios in a table or graphing on a coordinate plane and observing whether the graph is a straight line through the origin.

4C74F660DFE701317BC868A86D17958E.description: Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities.

4C74A4A0DFE701317BC768A86D17958E.description: Compute unit rates associated with ratios of fractions, including ratios of lengths, areas and other quantities measured in like or different units.
comments: For example, if a person walks 1/2 mile in each 1/4 hour, compute the unit rate as the complex fraction <sup>1/2</sup>/<sub>1/4</sub> miles per hour, equivalently 2 miles per hour.

4C7442A0DFE701317BC668A86D17958E.description: Analyze proportional relationships and use them to solve real-world and mathematical problems.

4C73B390DFE701317BC468A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area, volume and surface area of two- and three-dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms.

4C7357F0DFE701317BC368A86D17958E.description: Use facts about supplementary, complementary, vertical, and adjacent angles in a multi-step problem to write and solve simple equations for an unknown angle in a figure.

4C730D10DFE701317BC268A86D17958E.description: Know the formulas for the area and circumference of a circle and use them to solve problems; give an informal derivation of the relationship between the circumference and area of a circle.

4C72CAC0DFE701317BC168A86D17958E.description: Solve real-life and mathematical problems involving angle measure, area, surface area, and volume.

4C7285B0DFE701317BC068A86D17958E.description: Describe the two-dimensional figures that result from slicing three-dimensional figures, as in plane sections of right rectangular prisms and right rectangular pyramids.

4C723FE0DFE701317BBF68A86D17958E.description: Draw (freehand, with ruler and protractor, and with technology) geometric shapes with given conditions. Focus on constructing triangles from three measures of angles or sides, noticing when the conditions determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle.

4C71FA80DFE701317BBE68A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving scale drawings of geometric figures, including computing actual lengths and areas from a scale drawing and reproducing a scale drawing at a different scale.

4C71AF70DFE701317BBD68A86D17958E.description: Draw, construct, and describe geometrical figures and describe the relationships between them.

4C710BB0DFE701317BBB68A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

4C70AE50DFE701317BBA68A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
4C6F4100DFE701317BB668A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

4C6E8CC0DFE701317BB468A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Rhode Island Health Education Framework

50316870DFE70131826268A86D17958E.description: Work cooperatively when advocating for healthy individuals, families and schools.

503124D0DFE70131826168A86D17958E.description: Influence and support others in making positive health choices.

5030E130DFE70131826068A86D17958E.description: Identify barriers to effective communication of information, ideas, feelings and opinions about health issues.

5030A0B0DFE70131825F68A86D17958E.description: Analyze various communication methods needed to express health information and ideas accurately.

50305DB0DFE70131825E68A86D17958E.description: Discuss accurate information and express opinions about health issues.

503015E0DFE70131825D68A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate the ability to advocate for personal, family, community and environmental health.
comments: This standard deals specifically with a student's ability to use advocacy skills to maintain and improve his/her personal health as well as that of her/his family, community and environment.

502FCAA0DFE70131825C68A86D17958E.description: Develop a plan that addresses personal strengths, needs and health risks.

502F8110DFE70131825B68A86D17958E.description: Apply strategies and skills needed to attain personal health goals.

502F38A0DFE70131825A68A86D17958E.description: Predict how decisions regarding health behaviors have consequences for self or others.

502EE120DFE70131825968A86D17958E.description: Analyze how health-related decisions are influenced by individuals, family or community values.

502E7DC0DFE70131825868A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate the ability to apply a decision-making process to health issues and problems individually and collaboratively.

comments: This standard deals directly with goal setting and decision-making, both of which are fundamental in taking control over the direction of one's health.
502E2AB0DFE70131825768A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate the ability to use goal-setting and decision-making skills to enhance health.

502DD730DFE70131825668A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate strategies needed to manage conflict in healthy ways.

502D97E0DFE70131825568A86D17958E.description: Analyze the possible causes of conflict among youth in schools and communities.

502D57A0DFE70131825468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate refusal and negotiation skills needed to enhance health.

502D16F0DFE70131825368A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate communication skills needed to build and maintain healthy relationships.

502CD560DFE70131825268A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate ways to communicate care, consideration and respect of self and others.

502C9490DFE70131825168A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate healthy ways to express needs, wants and feelings.

502C4C10DFE70131825068A86D17958E.description: Describe how the behavior of family and peers affects interpersonal communication.

502C06F0DFE70131824F68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate effective verbal & non-verbal communication skills to enhance health.

502BC320DFE70131824E68A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate the ability to use interpersonal communication skills to enhance health.
comments: This standard focuses on effective communication which is fundamental to ensuring healthy relationships and interpreting one's own state of health.

502B8120DFE70131824D68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how information from peers influences and affects health choices.

502B3D60DFE70131824C68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the influence of technology on personal or family health.

502AF7F0DFE70131824B68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how positive and negative messages from media and other resources influence health behaviors.

502A9FF0DFE70131824A68A86D17958E.description: Describe the influence of cultural beliefs on health behaviors and the use of health services.

502A4940DFE70131824968A86D17958E.description: Students will analyze the influence of culture, media, technology and other factors on health.
comments: This standard focuses on the individual's ability to interpret how culture, media, technology and other factors that are not always defined as having a health focus can influence the individual's well-being (for example, the increasing amount of violence on TV has an impact on how society functions and in turn can affect individual behaviors as well as actions).

5029E4D0DFE70131824868A86D17958E.description: Develop and apply appropriate ways of managing conflict and specific stressful situations.

5029A430DFE70131824768A86D17958E.description: Identify and demonstrate ways to avoid and reduce threatening situations.

502960B0DFE70131824668A86D17958E.description: Develop injury prevention and management strategies for personal, family and community health.

502916B0DFE70131824568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate strategies to improve or maintain personal and family health.

5028B0C0DFE70131824468A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between safe and risky or harmful behaviors.

50286D00DFE70131824368A86D17958E.description: Analyze personal health habits to determine health strengths and risks.

50282CE0DFE70131824268A86D17958E.description: Explain the importance of assuming responsibility for personal health behaviors.

5027EB70DFE70131824168A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate the ability to practice health-enhancing behaviors and reduce health risks.
comments: This standard focuses on health-fostering behaviors that will preserve the individual.

5027AB00DFE70131824068A86D17958E.description: Explain roles played by different health providers.

502767F0DFE70131823F68A86D17958E.description: Describe situations requiring professional health services.

50272180DFE70131823E68A86D17958E.description: Compare the costs and validity of health products.

50268F90DFE70131823C68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how media influences the selection of health information, products and services.

50264B50DFE70131823B68A86D17958E.description: Utilize resources form home, school and community that provide valid health information.

50260920DFE70131823A68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the validity of health information, products, and services.

5025C4B0DFE70131823968A86D17958E.description: Students will demonstrate the ability to access valid health information and health promoting products and services.
comments: This standard deals with the external sources that are directly focused on an individual's well being, including specific health focused information (e.g. the food pyramid), products (e.g. cough medicine), and services and service providers (e.g. doctors).

50257E20DFE70131823868A86D17958E.description: Describe how lifestyle, family history, pathogens and other risk factors are related to the cause or prevention of disease and other health problems.

50252D60DFE70131823768A86D17958E.description: Explain how appropriate health care can prevent premature death and disability.

5024E710DFE70131823668A86D17958E.description: Describe ways to reduce risks related to early adolescent health problems.

5024A2E0DFE70131823568A86D17958E.description: Analyze how environment and personal health are interrelated.

50245FA0DFE70131823468A86D17958E.description: Describe how family, peers and environment influence the health of adolescents.

50241260DFE70131823368A86D17958E.description: Explain how health is influenced by the interaction of body systems.

5023A7F0DFE70131823268A86D17958E.description: Describe the interrelationship of mental, emotional, physical, social and physical health during adolescence.

501CDA40DFE70131823168A86D17958E.description: Explain the relationship between positive health behaviors and the prevention of injury, illness, disease and premature death.

501C8D40DFE70131823068A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the concepts related to health promotion and disease prevention as a foundation for a healthy life.
comments: This standard deals with the fundamental aspects of personal health and disease. This standard is probably the most dense standard in terms of health content.

document.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

4B560C70DFE701317A7468A86D17958E.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, fourths, and quarters, and use the phrases half of, fourth of, and quarter of. Describe the whole as two of, or four of the shares. Understand for these examples that decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares.

comments: Students do not need to learn formal names such as "right rectangular prism."
4B55C690DFE701317A7368A86D17958E.description: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, and quarter-circles) or three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, and right circular cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape.

4B5562C0DFE701317A7268A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between defining attributes (e.g., triangles are closed and three-sided) versus non-defining attributes (e.g., color, orientation, overall size); build and draw shapes to possess defining attributes.

4B551860DFE701317A7168A86D17958E.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

4B549300DFE701317A6F68A86D17958E.description: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.

4B540640DFE701317A6D68A86D17958E.description: Tell and write time in hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks.

4B538650DFE701317A6B68A86D17958E.description: Express the length of an object as a whole number of length units, by laying multiple copies of a shorter object (the length unit) end to end; understand that the length measurement of an object is the number of same-size length units that span it with no gaps or overlaps.
comments: Limit to contexts where the object being measured is spanned by a whole number of length units with no gaps or overlaps.

4B5334F0DFE701317A6A68A86D17958E.description: Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.

4B52D380DFE701317A6968A86D17958E.description: Measure lengths indirectly and by iterating length units.

4B522DA0DFE701317A6768A86D17958E.description: Subtract multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 from multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 (positive or zero differences), using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.

4B51F0C0DFE701317A6668A86D17958E.description: Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count; explain the reasoning used.

4B51B120DFE701317A6568A86D17958E.description: Add within 100, including adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number, and adding a two-digit number and a multiple of 10, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used. Understand that in adding two-digit numbers, one adds tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose a ten.

4B5170C0DFE701317A6468A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.

4B5127A0DFE701317A6368A86D17958E.description: Compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, and <.

4B50DB10DFE701317A6268A86D17958E.description: The numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine tens (and 0 ones).

4B509920DFE701317A6168A86D17958E.description: The numbers from 11 to 19 are composed of a ten and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

4B505500DFE701317A6068A86D17958E.description: 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a "ten."

4B500CF0DFE701317A5F68A86D17958E.description: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones. Understand the following as special cases:

4B4F6340DFE701317A5D68A86D17958E.description: Count to 120, starting at any number less than 120. In this range, read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral.

4B4EDF80DFE701317A5B68A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

4B4EA0D0DFE701317A5A68A86D17958E.description: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 + ? = 11, 5 = - 3, 6 + 6 = .
For example, which of the following equations are true and which are false? 6 = 6, 7 = 8 - 1, 5 + 2 = 2 + 5, 4 + 1 = 5 + 2.
4B4E61D0DFE701317A5968A86D17958E.description: Understand the meaning of the equal sign, and determine if equations involving addition and subtraction are true or false.

4B4E2430DFE701317A5868A86D17958E.description: Work with addition and subtraction equations.

4B4DE3F0DFE701317A5768A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10. Use strategies such as counting on; making ten (e.g., 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (e.g., 13 - 4 = 13 - 3 - 1 = 10 - 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 - 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).

4B4DA300DFE701317A5668A86D17958E.description: Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g., by counting on 2 to add 2).

4B4D07F0DFE701317A5468A86D17958E.description: Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem.
comments: For example, subtract 10 - 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.
Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
To add 2 + 6 + 4, the second two numbers can be added to make a ten, so 2 + 6 + 4 = 2 + 10 = 12. (Associative property of addition.)
If 8 + 3 = 11 is known, then 3 + 8 = 11 is also known. (Commutative property of addition.)
4B4CC6E0DFE701317A5368A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract.

4B4C8720DFE701317A5268A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

4B4C4620DFE701317A5168A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems that call for addition of three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

4B4C02E0DFE701317A5068A86D17958E.description: Use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

4B4BB9B0DFE701317A4F68A86D17958E.description: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.

4B4B0430DFE701317A4D68A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.
4B4AAB90DFE701317A4C68A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.

comments: Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
4B4946C0DFE701317A4868A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

4B48A330DFE701317A4668A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

43AB6200DFE701316D8268A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases, including those that signal contrast, addition, and other logical relationships (e.g., however, although, nevertheless, similarly, moreover, in addition).

43AA93D0DFE701316D8068A86D17958E.description: Recognize and explain the meaning of common idioms, adages, and proverbs.

43AA40F0DFE701316D7F68A86D17958E.description: Interpret figurative language, including similes and metaphors, in context.

43A9F0E0DFE701316D7E68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

43A9A3B0DFE701316D7D68A86D17958E.description: Consult reference materials (e.g., dictionaries, glossaries, thesauruses), both print and digital, to find the pronunciation and determine or clarify the precise meaning of key words and phrases.

43A95B00DFE701316D7C68A86D17958E.description: Use common, grade-appropriate Greek and Latin affixes and roots as clues to the meaning of a word (e.g., photograph, photosynthesis).

43A90FC0DFE701316D7B68A86D17958E.description: Use context (e.g., cause/effect relationships and comparisons in text) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
