43A81D70DFE701316D7868A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the varieties of English (e.g., dialects, registers) used in stories, dramas, or poems.

43A7CDE0DFE701316D7768A86D17958E.description: Expand, combine, and reduce sentences for meaning, reader/listener interest, and style.

43A77E80DFE701316D7668A86D17958E.description: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.

43A6CDF0DFE701316D7468A86D17958E.description: Spell grade-appropriate words correctly, consulting references as needed.

43A67C90DFE701316D7368A86D17958E.description: Use underlining, quotation marks, or italics to indicate titles of works.

43A622F0DFE701316D7268A86D17958E.description: Use a comma to set off the words yes and no (e.g., Yes, thank you), to set off a tag question from the rest of the sentence (e.g., It's true, isn't it?), and to indicate direct address (e.g., Is that you, Steve?).

43A5D630DFE701316D7168A86D17958E.description: Use a comma to separate an introductory element from the rest of the sentence.

43A589B0DFE701316D7068A86D17958E.description: Use punctuation to separate items in a series.

43A53B20DFE701316D6F68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

43A47E60DFE701316D6D68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and correct inappropriate shifts in verb tense.

43A434A0DFE701316D6C68A86D17958E.description: Use verb tense to convey various times, sequences, states, and conditions.

43A3EB70DFE701316D6B68A86D17958E.description: Form and use the perfect (e.g., I had walked; I have walked; I will have walked) verb tenses.

43A3A160DFE701316D6A68A86D17958E.description: Explain the function of conjunctions, prepositions, and interjections in general and their function in particular sentences.

43A351C0DFE701316D6968A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

43A265D0DFE701316D6668A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately a range of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases sufficient for reading, writing, speaking, and listening at the college and career readiness level; demonstrate independence in gathering vocabulary knowledge when encountering an unknown term important to comprehension or expression.

43A1ED10DFE701316D6568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

43A19380DFE701316D6468A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases by using context clues, analyzing meaningful word parts, and consulting general and specialized reference materials, as appropriate.

43A0BB30DFE701316D6268A86D17958E.description: Apply knowledge of language to understand how language functions in different contexts, to make effective choices for meaning or style, and to comprehend more fully when reading or listening.

43A02C20DFE701316D6068A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

439FE120DFE701316D5F68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

439F28B0DFE701316D5D68A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Language

439ED780DFE701316D5C68A86D17958E.description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, using formal English when appropriate to task and situation.

439E86D0DFE701316D5B68A86D17958E.description: Include multimedia components (e.g., graphics, sound) and visual displays in presentations when appropriate to enhance the development of main ideas or themes.

439E3B40DFE701316D5A68A86D17958E.description: Report on a topic or text or present an opinion, sequencing ideas logically and using appropriate facts and relevant, descriptive details to support main ideas or themes; speak clearly at an understandable pace.

439D9ED0DFE701316D5868A86D17958E.description: Summarize the points a speaker makes and explain how each claim is supported by reasons and evidence.

439D4390DFE701316D5768A86D17958E.description: Summarize a written text read aloud or information presented in diverse media and formats, including visually, quantitatively, and orally.

439CF5C0DFE701316D5668A86D17958E.description: Review the key ideas expressed and draw conclusions in light of information and knowledge gained from the discussions.

439C9D40DFE701316D5568A86D17958E.description: Pose and respond to specific questions by making comments that contribute to the discussion and elaborate on the remarks of others.

439C4870DFE701316D5468A86D17958E.description: Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions and carry out assigned roles.

439BE820DFE701316D5368A86D17958E.description: Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation and other information known about the topic to explore ideas under discussion.

439B8B10DFE701316D5268A86D17958E.description: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 5 topics and texts, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly.

439AB230DFE701316D4F68A86D17958E.description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and communicative tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

439A6680DFE701316D4E68A86D17958E.description: Make strategic use of digital media and visual displays of data to express information and enhance understanding of presentations.

439A0950DFE701316D4D68A86D17958E.description: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence such that listeners can follow the line of reasoning and the organization, development, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

43996570DFE701316D4B68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.

43991730DFE701316D4A68A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate information presented in diverse media and formats, including visually, quantitatively, and orally.

4398CD30DFE701316D4968A86D17958E.description: Prepare for and participate effectively in a range of conversations and collaborations with diverse partners, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.

439824F0DFE701316D4768A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Speaking and Listening

4397D920DFE701316D4668A86D17958E.description: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences.

439728F0DFE701316D4468A86D17958E.description: Apply grade 5 Reading standards to informational texts (e.g., "Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point[s]").

4396CB00DFE701316D4368A86D17958E.description: Apply grade 5 Reading standards to literature (e.g., "Compare and contrast two or more characters, settings, or events in a story or a drama, drawing on specific details in the text [e.g., how characters interact]").

43966520DFE701316D4268A86D17958E.description: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

43961ED0DFE701316D4168A86D17958E.description: Recall relevant information from experiences or gather relevant information from print and digital sources; summarize or paraphrase information in notes and finished work, and provide a list of sources.

4395D860DFE701316D4068A86D17958E.description: Conduct short research projects that use several sources to build knowledge through investigation of different aspects of a topic.

439591A0DFE701316D3F68A86D17958E.description: Research to Build and Present Knowledge

43954860DFE701316D3E68A86D17958E.description: With some guidance and support from adults, use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing as well as to interact and collaborate with others; demonstrate sufficient command of keyboarding skills to type a minimum of two pages in a single sitting.

4394F850DFE701316D3D68A86D17958E.description: With guidance and support from peers and adults, develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.

4394A440DFE701316D3C68A86D17958E.description: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development and organization are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
comments: (Grade-specific expectations for writing types are defined in standards 1—3 above.)

43940280DFE701316D3A68A86D17958E.description: Provide a conclusion that follows from the narrated experiences or events.

43938D30DFE701316D3968A86D17958E.description: Use concrete words and phrases and sensory details to convey experiences and events precisely.

43933100DFE701316D3868A86D17958E.description: Use a variety of transitional words, phrases, and clauses to manage the sequence of events.

4392D340DFE701316D3768A86D17958E.description: Use narrative techniques, such as dialogue, description, and pacing, to develop experiences and events or show the responses of characters to situations.

43928BB0DFE701316D3668A86D17958E.description: Orient the reader by establishing a situation and introducing a narrator and/or characters; organize an event sequence that unfolds naturally.

439240B0DFE701316D3568A86D17958E.description: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, descriptive details, and clear event sequences.

4391F490DFE701316D3468A86D17958E.description: Provide a concluding statement or section related to the information or explanation presented

4391A870DFE701316D3368A86D17958E.description: Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic.

43915900DFE701316D3268A86D17958E.description: Link ideas within and across categories of information using words, phrases, and clauses (e.g., in contrast, especially).

439101A0DFE701316D3168A86D17958E.description: Develop the topic with facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations, or other information and examples related to the topic.

4390B940DFE701316D3068A86D17958E.description: Introduce a topic clearly, provide a general observation and focus, and group related information logically; include formatting (e.g., headings), illustrations, and multimedia when useful to aiding comprehension.

439071B0DFE701316D2F68A86D17958E.description: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.

43902A40DFE701316D2E68A86D17958E.description: Provide a concluding statement or section related to the opinion presented.

438FD9D0DFE701316D2D68A86D17958E.description: Link opinion and reasons using words, phrases, and clauses (e.g., consequently, specifically).

438F7F20DFE701316D2C68A86D17958E.description: Provide logically ordered reasons that are supported by facts and details.

438F1FC0DFE701316D2B68A86D17958E.description: Introduce a topic or text clearly, state an opinion, and create an organizational structure in which ideas are logically grouped to support the writer's purpose.

438ED120DFE701316D2A68A86D17958E.description: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons and information

438DBC30DFE701316D2768A86D17958E.description: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.

438D1CB0DFE701316D2568A86D17958E.description: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

438CD0B0DFE701316D2468A86D17958E.description: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources, assess the credibility and accuracy of each source, and integrate the information while avoiding plagiarism.

438C8240DFE701316D2368A86D17958E.description: Conduct short as well as more sustained research projects based on focused questions, demonstrating understanding of the subject under investigation.

438C3330DFE701316D2268A86D17958E.description: Research to Build and Present Knowledge

438BE030DFE701316D2168A86D17958E.description: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing and to interact and collaborate with others.

438B8110DFE701316D2068A86D17958E.description: Develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.

438B25C0DFE701316D1F68A86D17958E.description: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

438A8160DFE701316D1D68A86D17958E.description: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, well-chosen details, and well-structured event sequences.

438A2250DFE701316D1C68A86D17958E.description: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas and information clearly and accurately through the effective selection, organization, and analysis of content.

4389B9B0DFE701316D1B68A86D17958E.description: Write arguments to support claims in an analysis of substantive topics or texts, using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.

43892620DFE701316D1968A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Writing

4388D920DFE701316D1868A86D17958E.description: Use context to confirm or self-correct word recognition and understanding, rereading as necessary.

43887790DFE701316D1768A86D17958E.description: Read on-level prose and poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression on successive readings

4387FDC0DFE701316D1668A86D17958E.description: Read on-level text with purpose and understanding.

4387B090DFE701316D1568A86D17958E.description: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.

43871550DFE701316D1368A86D17958E.description: Use combined knowledge of all letter-sound correspondences, syllabication patterns, and morphology (e.g., roots and affixes) to read accurately unfamiliar multisyllabic words in context and out of context.

4386C7F0DFE701316D1268A86D17958E.description: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.

4385D100DFE701316D0F68A86D17958E.description: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 4—5 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

438579E0DFE701316D0E68A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

43852370DFE701316D0D68A86D17958E.description: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.

4384C9C0DFE701316D0C68A86D17958E.description: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point(s).

43847660DFE701316D0B68A86D17958E.description: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or to solve a problem efficiently.

4383E320DFE701316D0968A86D17958E.description: Analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent.

43839730DFE701316D0868A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the overall structure (e.g., chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more texts.

43834CD0DFE701316D0768A86D17958E.description: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 5 topic or subject area.

438286A0DFE701316D0568A86D17958E.description: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text based on specific information in the text.

438231D0DFE701316D0468A86D17958E.description: Determine two or more main ideas of a text and explain how they are supported by key details; summarize the text.

4381E660DFE701316D0368A86D17958E.description: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.

43810550DFE701316D0068A86D17958E.description: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poetry, at the high end of the grades 4—5 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

4380ABE0DFE701316CFF68A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

437FFE10DFE701316CFD68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast stories in the same genre (e.g., mysteries and adventure stories) on their approaches to similar themes and topics.

437FA7C0DFE701316CFC68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how visual and multimedia elements contribute to the meaning, tone, or beauty of a text (e.g., graphic novel, multimedia presentation of fiction, folktale, myth, poem).

437F1630DFE701316CFA68A86D17958E.description: Describe how a narrator's or speaker's point of view influences how events are described.

437EBF80DFE701316CF968A86D17958E.description: Explain how a series of chapters, scenes, or stanzas fits together to provide the overall structure of a particular story, drama, or poem.

437E7350DFE701316CF868A86D17958E.description: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative language such as metaphors and similes.

437DD9F0DFE701316CF668A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast two or more characters, settings, or events in a story or drama, drawing on specific details in the text (e.g., how characters interact).

437D8C00DFE701316CF568A86D17958E.description: Determine a theme of a story, drama, or poem from details in the text, including how characters in a story or drama respond to challenges or how the speaker in a poem reflects upon a topic; summarize the text.

437D3AE0DFE701316CF468A86D17958E.description: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.

437C4500DFE701316CF168A86D17958E.description: Read and comprehend complex literary and informational texts independently and proficiently.

437BFAB0DFE701316CF068A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

437BB1D0DFE701316CEF68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how two or more texts address similar themes or topics in order to build knowledge or to compare the approaches the authors take.

437B6380DFE701316CEE68A86D17958E.description: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, including the validity of the reasoning as well as the relevance and sufficiency of the evidence.

437B10E0DFE701316CED68A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate content presented in diverse media and formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words.
comments: Please see "Research to Build and Present Knowledge" in Writing and "Comprehension and Collaboration" in Speaking and Listening for additional standards relevant to gathering, assessing, and applying information from print and digital sources.

437A8110DFE701316CEB68A86D17958E.description: Assess how point of view or purpose shapes the content and style of a text.

437A3870DFE701316CEA68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the structure of texts, including how specific sentences, paragraphs, and larger portions of the text (e.g., a section, chapter, scene, or stanza) relate to each other and the whole.

4379EF60DFE701316CE968A86D17958E.description: Interpret words and phrases as they are used in a text, including determining technical, connotative, and figurative meanings, and analyze how specific word choices shape meaning or tone.

43794240DFE701316CE768A86D17958E.description: Analyze how and why individuals, events, and ideas develop and interact over the course of a text.

4378F1B0DFE701316CE668A86D17958E.description: Determine central ideas or themes of a text and analyze their development; summarize the key supporting details and ideas.

43787320DFE701316CE568A86D17958E.description: Read closely to determine what the text says explicitly and to make logical inferences from it; cite specific textual evidence when writing or speaking to support conclusions drawn from the text.

43779A80DFE701316CE368A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Reading

4B7AEF80DFE701317AA868A86D17958E.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, thirds, half of, a third of, etc., and describe the whole as two halves, three thirds, four fourths. 4B7A0DA0DFE701317AA568A86D17958E.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

Understand that in adding or subtracting three-digit numbers, one adds or subtracts hundreds and hundreds, tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose or decompose tens or hundreds.

4B713FB0DFE701317A8A68A86D17958E.description: 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a "hundred."

comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

4B7010E0DFE701317A8668A86D17958E.description: Use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and up to 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends.

4B6FCEA0DFE701317A8568A86D17958E.description: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g., by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends.

4B6F8B00DFE701317A8468A86D17958E.description: Work with equal groups of objects to gain foundations for multiplication.

4B6F39F0DFE701317A8368A86D17958E.description: Fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies. By end of Grade 2, know from memory all sums of two one-digit numbers.
comments: See standard 1.OA.6 for a list of mental strategies.

4B6E9590DFE701317A8168A86D17958E.description: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve one- and two-step word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

4B6E4F60DFE701317A8068A86D17958E.description: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.

4B6DC1B0DFE701317A7E68A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

4B6D73F0DFE701317A7D68A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
4B6C2390DFE701317A7968A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

4B6B85F0DFE701317A7768A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

42920040DFE701316B2968A86D17958E.description: Identify the main purpose of a text, including what the author wants to answer, explain, or describe.

4291B210DFE701316B2868A86D17958E.description: Know and use various text features (e.g., captions, bold print, subheadings, glossaries, indexes, electronic menus, icons) to locate key facts or information in a text efficiently.

4290C0C0DFE701316B2568A86D17958E.description: Describe the connection between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text.

428F1040DFE701316B2068A86D17958E.description: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature, including stories and poetry, in the grades 2—3 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.

428C7430DFE701316B1868A86D17958E.description: Describe how words and phrases (e.g., regular beats, alliteration, rhymes, repeated lines) supply rhythm and meaning in a story, poem, or song.

428BD250DFE701316B1668A86D17958E.description: Describe how characters in a story respond to major events and challenges.

428B8770DFE701316B1568A86D17958E.description: Recount stories, including fables and folktales from diverse cultures, and determine their central message, lesson, or moral.

428A1250DFE701316B1168A86D17958E.description: Read and comprehend complex literary and informational texts independently and proficiently.

4289C740DFE701316B1068A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

42890F40DFE701316B0E68A86D17958E.description: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, including the validity of the reasoning as well as the relevance and sufficiency of the evidence.

4287CE30DFE701316B0A68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the structure of texts, including how specific sentences, paragraphs, and larger portions of the text (e.g., a section, chapter, scene, or stanza) relate to each other and the whole.

Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
AA13DBA5B1CE490BA268C9CBD9152AC9.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

0D79DC7467DF48DE880EC60874616833.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
2C3BF29C7A0A4894A42BAD4D58F889A8.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
9A728FFE624A43EBB7EB23E112CA0D1C.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

4B354380DFE701317A4368A86D17958E.description: Compose simple shapes to form larger shapes.
comments: For example, "Can you join these two triangles with full sides touching to make a rectangle?"

4B350380DFE701317A4268A86D17958E.description: Model shapes in the world by building shapes from components (e.g., sticks and clay balls) and drawing shapes.

4B34C200DFE701317A4168A86D17958E.description: Analyze and compare two- and three-dimensional shapes, in different sizes and orientations, using informal language to describe their similarities, differences, parts (e.g., number of sides and vertices/"corners") and other attributes (e.g., having sides of equal length).

4B346F10DFE701317A4068A86D17958E.description: Analyze, compare, create, and compose shapes.

4B341B90DFE701317A3F68A86D17958E.description: Identify shapes as two-dimensional (lying in a plane, "flat") or three-dimensional ("solid").

4B33C0A0DFE701317A3E68A86D17958E.description: Correctly name shapes regardless of their orientations or overall size.

4B338030DFE701317A3D68A86D17958E.description: Describe objects in the environment using names of shapes, and describe the relative positions of these objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, and next to.

4B333D60DFE701317A3C68A86D17958E.description: Identify and describe shapes (squares, circles, triangles, rectangles, hexagons, cubes, cones, cylinders, and spheres).

4B32AD30DFE701317A3A68A86D17958E.description: Classify objects into given categories; count the numbers of objects in each category and sort the categories by count.
comments: Limit category counts to be less than or equal to 10.

4B324C40DFE701317A3968A86D17958E.description: Classify objects and count the number of objects in each category.

4B320030DFE701317A3868A86D17958E.description: Directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute in common, to see which object has "more of"/"less of" the attribute, and describe the difference.
comments: For example, directly compare the heights of two children and describe one child as taller/shorter.

4B31BE90DFE701317A3768A86D17958E.description: Describe measurable attributes of objects, such as length or weight. Describe several measurable attributes of a single object.

4B30F540DFE701317A3468A86D17958E.description: Compose and decompose numbers from 11 to 19 into ten ones and some further ones, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each composition or decomposition by a drawing or equation (e.g., 18 = 10 + 8); understand that these numbers are composed of ten ones and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

4B30AB70DFE701317A3368A86D17958E.description: Work with numbers 11—19 to gain foundations for place value.

comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.
4B305F80DFE701317A3268A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten

4B2FD410DFE701317A3068A86D17958E.description: For any number from 1 to 9, find the number that makes 10 when added to the given number, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record the answer with a drawing or equation.

4B2F85A0DFE701317A2F68A86D17958E.description: Decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way, e.g., by using objects or drawings, and record each decomposition by a drawing or equation (e.g., 5 = 2 + 3 and 5 = 4 + 1).

4B2F3830DFE701317A2E68A86D17958E.description: Solve addition and subtraction word problems, and add and subtract within 10, e.g., by using objects or drawings to represent the problem.

4B2EDE20DFE701317A2D68A86D17958E.description: Represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, sounds (e.g., claps), acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations.
comments: Drawings need not show details, but should show the mathematics in the problem (This applies wherever drawings are mentioned in the Standards.)

4B2E9440DFE701317A2C68A86D17958E.description: Understand addition as putting together and adding to, and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from.

4B2E11D0DFE701317A2A68A86D17958E.description: Compare two numbers between 1 and 10 presented as written numerals.

comments: Include groups with up to ten objects.
4B2DCE50DFE701317A2968A86D17958E.description: Identify whether the number of objects in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to the number of objects in another group, e.g., by using matching and counting strategies.

4B2D4240DFE701317A2768A86D17958E.description: Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 20 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 10 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1—20, count out that many objects.

4B2CDB40DFE701317A2668A86D17958E.description: Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.

4B2C8E60DFE701317A2568A86D17958E.description: Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.

4B2C4760DFE701317A2468A86D17958E.description: When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object.

4B2C09F0DFE701317A2368A86D17958E.description: Understand the relationship between numbers and quantities; connect counting to cardinality.

4B2BCBE0DFE701317A2268A86D17958E.description: Count to tell the number of objects.

4B2B8C60DFE701317A2168A86D17958E.description: Write numbers from 0 to 20. Represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0-20 (with 0 representing a count of no objects).

4B2B4A80DFE701317A2068A86D17958E.description: Count forward beginning from a given number within the known sequence (instead of having to begin at 1).

4B2AF150DFE701317A1F68A86D17958E.description: Count to 100 by ones and by tens.

4B2A9680DFE701317A1E68A86D17958E.description: Know number names and the count sequence.

document.title: Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts/Literacy

442B80E0DFE701316E5268A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases; gather vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.

442AF480DFE701316E5168A86D17958E.description: Distinguish among the connotations (associations) of words with similar denotations (definitions) (e.g., stingy, scrimping, economical, unwasteful, thrifty).

442A81C0DFE701316E5068A86D17958E.description: Use the relationship between particular words (e.g., cause/effect, part/whole, item/category) to better understand each of the words.

442A1830DFE701316E4F68A86D17958E.description: Interpret figures of speech (e.g., personification) in context.

4429C1E0DFE701316E4E68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

44296A70DFE701316E4D68A86D17958E.description: Verify the preliminary determination of the meaning of a word or phrase (e.g., by checking the inferred meaning in context or in a dictionary).

442914A0DFE701316E4C68A86D17958E.description: Consult reference materials (e.g., dictionaries, glossaries, thesauruses), both print and digital, to find the pronunciation of a word or determine or clarify its precise meaning or its part of speech.

4428A310DFE701316E4B68A86D17958E.description: Use common, grade-appropriate Greek or Latin affixes and roots as clues to the meaning of a word (e.g., audience, auditory, audible).

44283B10DFE701316E4A68A86D17958E.description: Use context (e.g., the overall meaning of a sentence or paragraph; a word's position or function in a sentence) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.

4427EBB0DFE701316E4968A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 6 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.

44274BA0DFE701316E4768A86D17958E.description: Maintain consistency in style and tone.

4426F600DFE701316E4668A86D17958E.description: Vary sentence patterns for meaning, reader/listener interest, and style.

44269060DFE701316E4568A86D17958E.description: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.

442571D0DFE701316E4268A86D17958E.description: Use punctuation (commas, parentheses, dashes) to set off nonrestrictive/parenthetical elements.

44251350DFE701316E4168A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

4424B050DFE701316E4068A86D17958E.description: Recognize variations from standard English in their own and others' writing and speaking, and identify and use strategies to improve expression in conventional language.

44245D60DFE701316E3F68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and correct vague pronouns (i.e., ones with unclear or ambiguous antecedents).

44240680DFE701316E3E68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and correct inappropriate shifts in pronoun number and person.

44234600DFE701316E3C68A86D17958E.description: Ensure that pronouns are in the proper case (subjective, objective, possessive).

4422C390DFE701316E3B68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

442181C0DFE701316E3768A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately a range of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases sufficient for reading, writing, speaking, and listening at the college and career readiness level; demonstrate independence in gathering vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.

44211F90DFE701316E3668A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

4420C900DFE701316E3568A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases by using context clues, analyzing meaningful word parts, and consulting general and specialized reference materials, as appropriate.

44201930DFE701316E3368A86D17958E.description: Apply knowledge of language to understand how language functions in different contexts, to make effective choices for meaning or style, and to comprehend more fully when reading or listening.

441F5550DFE701316E3168A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

441EF960DFE701316E3068A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

441E3C20DFE701316E2E68A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Language

441DCA10DFE701316E2D68A86D17958E.description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

441D7220DFE701316E2C68A86D17958E.description: Include multimedia components (e.g., graphics, images, music, sound) and visual displays in presentations to clarify information.

441CF2D0DFE701316E2B68A86D17958E.description: Present claims and findings, sequencing ideas logically and using pertinent descriptions, facts, and details to accentuate main ideas or themes; use appropriate eye contact, adequate volume, and clear pronunciation.

441C23F0DFE701316E2968A86D17958E.description: Delineate a speaker's argument and specific claims, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.

441BCDC0DFE701316E2868A86D17958E.description: Interpret information presented in diverse media and formats (e.g., visually, quantitatively, orally) and explain how it contributes to a topic, text, or issue under study.

441B7E60DFE701316E2768A86D17958E.description: Review the key ideas expressed and demonstrate understanding of multiple perspectives through reflection and paraphrasing.

441B26E0DFE701316E2668A86D17958E.description: Pose and respond to specific questions with elaboration and detail by making comments that contribute to the topic, text, or issue under discussion.

441AD010DFE701316E2568A86D17958E.description: Follow rules for collegial discussions, set specific goals and deadlines, and define individual roles as needed.

441A7500DFE701316E2468A86D17958E.description: Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.

441A11F0DFE701316E2368A86D17958E.description: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 6 topics, texts, and issues, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly.

4418F510DFE701316E2068A86D17958E.description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and communicative tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

44189370DFE701316E1F68A86D17958E.description: Make strategic use of digital media and visual displays of data to express information and enhance understanding of presentations.

441838E0DFE701316E1E68A86D17958E.description: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence such that listeners can follow the line of reasoning and the organization, development, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

44177DA0DFE701316E1C68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.

441718D0DFE701316E1B68A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate information presented in diverse media and formats, including visually, quantitatively, and orally.

4416BD80DFE701316E1A68A86D17958E.description: Prepare for and participate effectively in a range of conversations and collaborations with diverse partners, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.

44160910DFE701316E1868A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Speaking and Listening

4415B7D0DFE701316E1768A86D17958E.description: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for reflection and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences.

44151250DFE701316E1568A86D17958E.description: Draw evidence from informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

4414A7D0DFE701316E1468A86D17958E.description: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources, using search terms effectively; assess the credibility and accuracy of each source; and quote or paraphrase the data and conclusions of others while avoiding plagiarism and following a standard format for citation.

44144950DFE701316E1368A86D17958E.description: Conduct short research projects to answer a question (including a self-generated question), drawing on several sources and generating additional related, focused questions that allow for multiple avenues of exploration.

4413EAB0DFE701316E1268A86D17958E.description: Research to Build and Present Knowledge

44138C50DFE701316E1168A86D17958E.description: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing and present the relationships between information and ideas clearly and efficiently.

44133070DFE701316E1068A86D17958E.description: With some guidance and support from peers and adults, develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach, focusing on how well purpose and audience have been addressed.

(e.g. Galapagos Islands, Hawaiian Islands, Australia, geographic isolation, adaptive radiation).

document.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

4BFF7630DFE701317B2768A86D17958E.description: Compare two decimals to hundredths by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two decimals refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual model.

4BFF3540DFE701317B2668A86D17958E.description: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100.
comments: For example, rewrite 0.62 as 62/100; describe a length as 0.62 meters; locate 0.62 on a number line diagram.

4BFEF180DFE701317B2568A86D17958E.description: Express a fraction with denominator 10 as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100, and use this technique to add two fractions with respective denominators 10 and 100.
comments: Students who can generate equivalent fractions can develop strategies for adding fractions with unlike denominators in general. But addition and subtraction with unlike denominators in general is not a requirement at this grade.
For example, express 3/10 as 30/100, and add 3/10 + 4/100 = 34/100.

4BFEAEE0DFE701317B2468A86D17958E.description: Understand decimal notation for fractions, and compare decimal fractions.

comments: For example, if each person at a party will eat 3/8 of a pound of roast beef, and there will be 5 people at the party, how many pounds of roast beef will be needed? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
4BFE63B0DFE701317B2368A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

4BFE1550DFE701317B2268A86D17958E.description: Understand a multiple of a/b as a multiple of 1/b, and use this understanding to multiply a fraction by a whole number.
comments: For example, use a visual fraction model to express 3 × (2/5) as 6 × (1/5), recognizing this product as 6/5. (In general, n × (a/b) = (n × a)/b.)
For example, use a visual fraction model to represent 5/4 as the product 5 × (1/4), recording the conclusion by the equation 5/4 = 5 × (1/4).
4BFDD390DFE701317B2168A86D17958E.description: Understand a fraction a/b as a multiple of 1/b.

4BFD9210DFE701317B2068A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction by a whole number.

4BFD4F00DFE701317B1F68A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and having like denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

4BFD0A70DFE701317B1E68A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, e.g., by replacing each mixed number with an equivalent fraction, and/or by using properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

4BFCC090DFE701317B1D68A86D17958E.description: Decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way, recording each decomposition by an equation. Justify decompositions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

4BFC6890DFE701317B1C68A86D17958E.description: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts referring to the same whole.

4BFC2790DFE701317B1B68A86D17958E.description: Understand a fraction a/b with a > 1 as a sum of fractions 1/b.

4BFBE540DFE701317B1A68A86D17958E.description: Build fractions from unit fractions by applying and extending previous understandings of operations on whole numbers.

4BFB9BB0DFE701317B1968A86D17958E.description: Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators, e.g., by creating common denominators or numerators, or by comparing to a benchmark fraction such as 1/2. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

4BFB4B60DFE701317B1868A86D17958E.description: Explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to a fraction (n × a)/(n × b) by using visual fraction models, with attention to how the number and size of the parts differ even though the two fractions themselves are the same size. Use this principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions.

4BFAFA80DFE701317B1768A86D17958E.description: Extend understanding of fraction equivalence and ordering.

comments: Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100

4BFA4030DFE701317B1568A86D17958E.description: Recognize a line of symmetry for a two-dimensional figure as a line across the figure such that the figure can be folded along the line into matching parts. Identify line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry.

An angle that turns through 1/360 of a circle is called a "one-degree angle," and can be used to measure angles.

4BF7CC30DFE701317B0C68A86D17958E.description: Recognize angles as geometric shapes that are formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint, and understand concepts of angle measurement:

4BF785F0DFE701317B0B68A86D17958E.description: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of angle and measure angles.

comments: For example, from a line plot find and interpret the difference in length between the longest and shortest specimens in an insect collection.

4BF72F50DFE701317B0A68A86D17958E.description: Apply the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real world and mathematical problems.

comments: For example, know that 1 ft is 12 times as long as 1 in. Express the length of a 4 ft snake as 48 in. Generate a conversion table for feet and inches listing the number pairs (1, 12), (2, 24), (3, 36), …

4BF65210DFE701317B0768A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving measurement and conversion of measurements from a larger unit to a smaller unit.

4BF3E380DFE701317AFF68A86D17958E.description: Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

4BF390E0DFE701317AFE68A86D17958E.description: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit whole number, and multiply two two-digit numbers, using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

4BF34E90DFE701317AFD68A86D17958E.description: Fluently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.

4BF30C20DFE701317AFC68A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.

4BF519A0DFE701317B0368A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.

4BF4D130DFE701317B0268A86D17958E.description: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form. Compare two multi-digit numbers based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

4BF47F10DFE701317B0168A86D17958E.description: Recognize that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right.
comments: For example, recognize that 700 ÷ 70 = 10 by applying concepts of place value and division.

4BF42EF0DFE701317B0068A86D17958E.description: Generalize place value understanding for multi-digit whole numbers.

4BF2C6C0DFE701317AFB68A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

4BF27CF0DFE701317AFA68A86D17958E.description: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself.
comments: For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 1, generate terms in the resulting sequence and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate in this way.

4BF1DEF0DFE701317AF868A86D17958E.description: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1—100. Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1—100 is a multiple of a given one-digit number. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1—100 is prime or composite.

4BF199E0DFE701317AF768A86D17958E.description: Gain familiarity with factors and multiples.

4BF14C20DFE701317AF668A86D17958E.description: Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.

4BF0FF40DFE701317AF568A86D17958E.description: Multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem, distinguishing multiplicative comparison from additive comparison.

4BF0A930DFE701317AF468A86D17958E.description: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison, e.g., interpret 35 = 5 × 7 as a statement that 35 is 5 times as many as 7 and 7 times as many as 5. Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.

4BF05CA0DFE701317AF368A86D17958E.description: Use the four operations with whole numbers to solve problems.

4BEFC360DFE701317AF168A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

4BEF7310DFE701317AF068A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
4BEE0E20DFE701317AEC68A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

4BED6B60DFE701317AEA68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
